summary: Mexico lets citizens of more than 60 countries and territories — including the US, Canada, the UK, the EU, Japan and much of Latin America — visit visa-free for up to 180 days, waives its visa for anyone holding a valid US visa, and offers a free electronic authorization (SAE) for air arrivals from Russia, Turkey and Ukraine.

primarySources.name: Instituto Nacional de Migración (INM) — National Migration Institute
Secretaría de Relaciones Exteriores (SRE) — Mexican consular network

declarations.name: FMM (Forma Migratoria Múltiple) — land arrivals only
declarations.text: At international airports you no longer fill in an FMM: the immigration officer stamps your passport with your expected departure date, and you can download the digital FMM (FMMd) afterwards. Note the date in the stamp — that, not 180 days, is your permitted stay. If you enter by land, you must present a completed FMM at the immigration filter.

currencyLimits.text: Anyone entering or leaving Mexico with more than USD 10,000 (or the equivalent) in cash, cheques or other monetary documents must declare it to customs. Carrying the money is not an offence; failing to declare it is fined 20–40% of the amount above USD 10,000, and an undeclared amount over USD 30,000 can mean 3 months to 6 years in prison and forfeiture of the excess.

source.name: ANAM — Declaración de dinero (cash declaration)

notes: The Government of Canada says goods worth more than USD 500 must be declared and that Mexico has strict rules on importing weapons, vehicles, cigarettes and alcohol. The UK FCDO says goods to declare must be declared online before you travel, or they may be seized and you could be fined.

Canada's travel advice says travellers aged 18 or over can bring into Mexico up to 20 packs of cigarettes, 25 cigars or 200 grams of tobacco, 3 litres of alcoholic beverages and 6 litres of wine; bringing more means a hefty import tax, even if you declare it.

Australia's Smartraveller says it is illegal to carry firearms or ammunition without a permit, including in Mexican waters; apply for a permit at a Mexican embassy or consulate before you arrive. Canada's travel advice says anyone entering Mexico with a firearm or ammunition without prior written authorization from the Mexican authorities is subject to imprisonment.
The UK FCDO says it is illegal to bring e-cigarettes, vaping devices and solutions into Mexico; customs officials will confiscate them and could fine or detain you.

payments.text: Australia's Smartraveller says most international hotels and tourist facilities accept credit and debit cards, ATMs are widely available in cities and towns, US dollars are widely accepted in holiday resort areas, and you should carry cash if travelling to rural areas.

safety.text: Safety varies sharply by state. The UK government advises against all but essential travel to all or parts of several states, including Zacatecas, Michoacán, Sinaloa, Tamaulipas, Chihuahua and parts of Baja California and Guanajuato, because of organised-crime violence. Risks are lower in tourist areas, though sexual offences have been reported there too. Check the advice for every state on your route and avoid travelling in higher-risk areas at night.

tips.text: Mexico is not one uniform risk level. Several states are under advice against all but essential travel, while risks are lower in the main tourist areas. Check advice for each state on your itinerary, not just the country page.
Entry to Mexico is free for visa-free tourists. Air arrivals no longer fill in an FMM, and third-party websites selling "Mexico tourist cards" or "entry registrations" are unnecessary.
180 days is the legal maximum, not a guarantee. Check the number of days the officer writes in your stamp before leaving the desk, and ask for more if your trip needs it.
Australia's Smartraveller advises drinking boiled water or bottled water with sealed lids and avoiding ice cubes in Mexico.

faq.question: Do US citizens need a visa for Mexico?
faq.answer: No. US citizens can visit Mexico visa-free for tourism or business for up to 180 days. The immigration officer decides the exact number of days and records it in your passport stamp. It is no longer an automatic 180.

faq.question: I have a US visa — do I still need a Mexican visa?
faq.answer: No. Any traveler holding a valid visa for the United States (or Canada, the UK, Japan or a Schengen country) is exempt from the Mexican visitor visa and can enter visa-free for up to 180 days, regardless of nationality.

faq.question: Is the FMM tourist card still required?
faq.answer: Only if you enter by land: INM requires a completed FMM at land crossings. At international airports there is no form to fill in — your passport stamp, showing your expected departure date, is the proof of legal entry, and you can download the digital FMM (FMMd) during your stay.

faq.question: What is Mexico's SAE electronic authorization?
faq.answer: The SAE (Sistema de Autorización Electrónica) is a free online authorization that lets citizens of Russia, Turkey and Ukraine fly to Mexico without a consular visa. It is valid for 30 days for a single air entry, allows a stay of up to 180 days, and cannot be used at land or sea borders.

faq.question: How long can I stay in Mexico as a tourist?
faq.answer: Up to 180 days if the immigration officer grants it — officers now often stamp shorter periods matched to your ticket and plans. The days granted appear in your entry stamp; overstaying leads to fines on exit.
